title: The Honey and the Gall
excerpt: Nobody falls in one step. Proverbs 7 watches a slow-motion fall, and shows the way out: run, and receive the grace that meets us after.

blocks.text: Nobody falls in one step.

If you've ever watched someone's life come apart through a moral failure, an affair, a hidden habit, a double life, you may have wondered how it could possibly have happened. They were a good person. They loved God. They would never have done *that.*

Proverbs 7 is the Bible's answer, and it reads like a slow-motion replay. The writer stands at his window, looks down at the street, and watches a young man walk toward the worst decision of his life. And what's startling is how quiet it all is. There's no moment where the young man decides to wreck everything. There's just a series of small steps, each one almost reasonable, until the last one isn't small at all.
Let's watch it together. Slowly.
Step One: He Chose the Route
"He was going down the street near her corner, walking along in the direction of her house" (Proverbs 7:8).

Read that sentence again and notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say he planned anything. It doesn't say he intended to sin. He's just *walking.* But look at where. Near her corner. In the direction of her house.

He didn't have to take that street. He had other options. And whatever his reasons were, the Bible doesn't ask what he was thinking. It just notes where his feet were pointed. The fall began long before the fall, at the moment he chose a route that would make it easy.

This is where most of us deceive ourselves. We think temptation is something that ambushes us. More often, we walk toward it, a little at a time, and call it coincidence. The late-night scroll we "just happened" to start. The coworker we've been confiding in a bit more than we should. The message we replied to when we could have let it go. The app we installed "just to look." Nobody stumbles into it. The path is usually chosen first.
Step Two: It Was Getting Dark
"...at twilight, as the day was fading, as the dark of night set in" (7:9).

Of course it was dark. Temptation loves the dark. Not just the hour, but the conditions: when we're tired, when we're lonely, when no one is checking in, when the day has worn our defenses down. The same person who would never be tempted at noon, surrounded by friends, may be defenseless at midnight, alone, scrolling, worn out.

It's worth asking yourself: when are you most vulnerable? Not the dramatic moments, but the ordinary ones. Tired. Bored. Stressed. Feeling unseen. Whatever the hour is, that's where the guard needs to be posted.
Step Three: A Voice That Sounded Right
Then she appears, and notice how she talks. She doesn't sound sinister. She sounds *warm.*

She starts with religious language: "Today I fulfilled my vows" (7:14). In other words, *I'm a spiritual person too.* Then comes flattery: "I came out to meet you; I looked for you and have found you!" (7:15). You're special. You were wanted. Then reassurance: "My husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey" (7:19). It's safe. No one will know.

Look at what the voice offers. Connection. Being noticed. A sense of significance. Safety. Almost all of it is something he might genuinely have wanted. Sin rarely offers something we don't want. It offers something we do, in a way that will cost far more than it's worth.

And that final promise, *no one will know*, is the oldest lie there is. As the previous chapter says, "your ways are in full view of the LORD, and he examines all your paths" (5:21). The only person this secrecy protects is the one doing the hiding.
Step Four: All at Once

"All at once he followed her like an ox going to the slaughter, like a deer stepping into a noose till an arrow pierces its liver, like a bird darting into a snare, little knowing it will cost him his life" (7:22–23).
*All at once.* That's the phrase to catch. It feels sudden, but only because we weren't watching the steps. The falling looks like a moment. It was actually a road.

And look at the last phrase: *little knowing.* He didn't know what it would cost. Nobody does. The animal doesn't see the trap. It sees the grain. The cost is always hidden at the moment of choosing and obvious afterward.
The Honey and the Gall
Earlier, in chapter 5, the father puts it another way:

verses: For the lips of the adulterous woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil; but in the end she is bitter as gall, sharp as a double-edged sword.

blocks.text: *Honey* now. *Gall* later. That's the whole deal. The early part is real, sweetness, attention, a rush. Proverbs doesn't pretend otherwise. But the end of the story is bitterness: broken trust, shattered marriages, wounded children, lost ministries, years of regret. Verses 11–12 imagine a man at the end of his life groaning, "How I hated discipline! How my heart spurned correction!"

And chapter 6 asks a question no one can answer in the way they'd like: "Can a man scoop fire into his lap without his clothes being burned? Can a man walk on hot coals without his feet being scorched?" (6:27–28). The problem isn't that we don't know the warning. It's that we think we'll be the exception. We believe we're stronger, smarter, more careful. We aren't.

A quick word: Proverbs was written to a young man, and the tempter in these passages is a woman. But the pattern doesn't belong to any one gender, any one kind of sin, or any one stage of life. It's true of the married woman who finds herself confiding in a coworker, the man who discovers pornography, the teenager lured by someone online, the husband and wife pulling quietly apart. Emotional affairs, secret habits, and porn aren't lesser versions of this story. They're early chapters of it.
God Isn't Against Joy
Before going further, I want to push back on a misreading. It would be easy to hear all of this and conclude that the Bible just wants to take pleasure away.

It's the opposite. Right in the middle of these warnings, the father says: "Drink water from your own cistern, running water from your own well... May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth... may you ever be intoxicated with her love" (5:15–19). God isn't prudish. He designed desire, and He designed it for a purpose: deep, faithful, committed love. The fence around it isn't there to deprive us. It's there to protect something precious.
Counterfeits only ever offer a sliver of what the real thing is meant to give.
Run
So what do you do?
Proverbs' answer is blunt and simple: "Keep to a path far from her, do not go near the door of her house" (5:8). Not *carefully approach.* Not *test your limits.* Stay far.
The New Testament says it in even fewer words: "Flee from sexual immorality" (1 Corinthians 6:18). The word is *flee.* Run. Not "resist" or "debate." Run.

The best example is Joseph, who was repeatedly pressured by his master's wife in Egypt. When she finally grabbed his cloak, he didn't stay to argue or negotiate. He left it in her hand and ran out of the house (Genesis 39:12). Not because he was weak, but because he was wise. He knew some battles are won by leaving.
In practice, fleeing might mean:

items: **Changing the route.** Deleting the app, blocking the number, ending the lunches, setting up filters, putting your phone out of the bedroom.
**Not being alone in the dark.** Telling someone, a friend, a spouse, a pastor, someone who can ask you directly how you're doing.
**Dealing with what's underneath.** Loneliness, resentment, feeling unseen. Temptation rarely starts in desire. It starts in a need that's going unmet.
**Filling the gap with something real.** Real friendships, real marriage, real worship. Sin loses its pull when the soul is nourished elsewhere.

blocks.text: If You've Already Fallen
If you've read this with a sinking feeling because you aren't at the beginning of the story but somewhere in the middle or after the end, I want you to hear something clearly.

There's a story in John 8. A woman is dragged into the street, caught in adultery, and thrown at Jesus' feet by men holding stones. Everyone knows what the law says. And Jesus, who was without sin, the only one with the right to throw a stone, says, "Neither do I condemn you." Then He adds, "Go now and leave your life of sin" (John 8:11).

Look at the order. Grace first. *Then* the call to change. He doesn't wait for her to clean herself up before showing mercy. And He doesn't use mercy as an excuse to leave her where she was. Both are true.

"Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). Your past isn't too far gone. The cross covers this too. Confess it, to God and to someone you trust ("confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed," James 5:16), turn from it, and let Him begin the repair. It may take time. Consequences may remain. But shame isn't His plan for you. Restoration is.
And if you're carrying shame from something done *to* you, that isn't yours to carry. It was never your fault.
The honey is always sweet at first. The gall always comes later. But there's a table where the sweetness doesn't turn bitter, and Jesus is already setting it.

items: What "route" are you walking right now? Is there a habit, a friendship, an app, or a pattern that is quietly pointing you toward somewhere you know you shouldn't go? What would it look like to change direction today, before the last step?
When are you most vulnerable? Think about the time of day, emotional state, or circumstance where your defenses are lowest. What one safeguard or person could you put in place around that moment?
Is there something you've been hiding that needs to be brought into the light? What would it take to tell God, and one trusted person, the truth this week?

blocks.text: Lord, You see every road I walk and every step I take. Forgive me for the times I've walked toward what I knew was wrong. Give me wisdom to see the steps before the fall, and courage to run when I should. Where I've already fallen, meet me with the mercy You showed the woman in the street, and begin to heal what's broken. Teach me to find in You what I've looked for everywhere else. Amen.
